ety.text: Unknown, with various theories as below. Compare English blizz (“violent rainstorm”), dialectal English bliz (“violent blow”); one etymology, from Midlands English dialect, seems to be ultimately from Old English blysa (“blaze”). Etymology theories * The earliest written use of blizzard as a term to describe a severe snowstorm, spelled blizard, was in the Estherville, Iowa's Northern Vindicator on 23 April 1870. O.C. Bates, neologistic editor of the Northern Vindicator, used it for the terrific snowstorms in the state that spring.

Pseudo-Germanism, derived from a clipping of blitzkrieg, from German Blitzkrieg (literally “lightning war”). The German word Blitz (“lightning”) lacks the "sudden attack" senses that the English word has.

senses.d: A sudden attack, especially an air raid; usually with reference to the Blitz.
A swift and overwhelming attack or effort.
ex: We embarked on a publicity blitz, putting posters and flyers all around town.
He [Yoshihide Suga] seems to be counting on a media blitz with feel-good effects around the Games to improve his sagging popularity.

senses.d: A play in which additional defenders beyond the defensive linemen rush the passer.
The act of blending or puréeing food using a blender or processor.
An occurrence in which large numbers of fish, typically striped bass or bluefish, feed on a school of baitfish, typically one in which the occurrence can be seen from the surface.
To attack quickly or suddenly, as by an air raid or similar action.
To perform a blitz.
ex: The Washington High defense almost always blitzes on third down.

senses.d: To purée or chop (food products) using a food processor or blender.
ex: To make nut roast, you have to blitz the nuts in the food processor before adding the parsley and breadcrumbs.

senses.d: To do something quickly or in one session.

ety.text: Ultimately from Latin lampades, possibly through a derivative of the Late Latin verb lampō, lampāre, with later alterations within early Romance, or from the related lampada. The prefix re- indicates the idea of repetition, hence lightning striking over and over again.

From Middle English bliss, from Old English bliss, variant of earlier blīds, blīþs (“joy, gladness”), from Proto-West Germanic *blīþisi (“joy, goodness, kindness”).

senses.d: Perfect happiness.
ex: The afternoon at the spa was utter bliss.
Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive, / But to be young was very heaven!

senses.d: To feel bliss; (by extension) to reach a state of bliss or ecstasy.
ex: I'm still blissing out after our date. I had a great time.

From Middle English blynd, from Old English blind, from Proto-West Germanic *blind, from Proto-Germanic *blindaz. Cognate with Danish, Dutch, German, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish blind, Faroese and Icelandic blindur.

senses.d: Unable to see, or only partially able to see.
ex: Even a blind hen sometimes finds a grain of corn.
Braille is a writing system for the blind.

senses.d: Failing to recognize, acknowledge or perceive.
ex: The lovers were blind to each other’s faults.
Authors are blind to their own defects.

senses.d: Having little or no visibility.
ex: a blind path
a blind ditch

senses.d: Closed at one end; having a dead end; exitless.
ex: a blind alley
a blind fistula

senses.d: Having no openings for light or passage; both dark and exitless.
ex: a blind wall
a blind alley

senses.d: Able to be fixed without access to one end.
ex: a blind rivet

senses.d: Smallest or slightest.
ex: I shouted, but he didn’t take a blind bit of notice.
We pulled and pulled, but it didn't make a blind bit of difference.

senses.d: Without any prior knowledge.
ex: He took a blind guess at which fork in the road would take him to the airport.
I went into the meeting totally blind, so I really didn’t have a clue what I was talking about.

senses.d: Unconditional; without regard to evidence, logic, reality, accidental mistakes, extenuating circumstances, etc.
ex: blind deference

senses.d: Using blinded study design, wherein information is purposely limited to prevent bias.

senses.d: A movable covering for a window to keep out light, made of cloth or of narrow slats that can block light or allow it to pass.
ex: A blind bearing the monogram G.V.T. is pulled down over the waiting room window as if still in mourning for the passing of the railway.
Light filtered in through the blinds of the french windows. It made tremulous stripes along the scrubbed pine floor.

senses.d: A destination sign mounted on a public transport vehicle displaying the route destination, number, name and/or via points, etc.
A place where people can hide in order to observe wildlife.

senses.d: Something to mislead the eye or the understanding, or to conceal some covert deed or design; a subterfuge, deception.

A hiding place.

So, when the watchful shepherd, from the blind,
Wounds with a random shaft the careless hind

senses.d: The blindside.
No score.
A forced bet: the small blind or the big blind.
ex: The blinds are $10 and $20, and the ante is $1.

senses.d: A player who is forced to pay such a bet.
ex: The blinds immediately folded when I reraised.

senses.d: To make temporarily or permanently blind.
ex: The light was so bright that for a moment he was blinded.
Don’t wave that pencil in my face—do you want to blind me?

senses.d: To curse, swear, use foul language
To darken; to obscure to the eye or understanding; to conceal.
ex: The state of the controversy between us he endeavored, with all his art, to blind and confound.

senses.d: To cover with a thin coating of sand and fine gravel, for example a road newly paved, in order that the joints between the stones may be filled.
Without seeing; unseeingly.

senses.d: Without looking at the cards dealt.

ety.text: From Middle English blynken, blenken, from Old English *blincan (suggested by causative verb blenċan (“to deceive”); > English blench), from Proto-Germanic *blinkaną, a variant of *blīkaną (“to gleam, shine”). Cognate with Dutch blinken (“to glitter, shine”), German blinken (“to flash, blink”), Danish blinke (“to flash, twinkle, wink, blink”), Swedish blinka (“to flash, blink, twinkle, wink, blink”). Related to blank, blick, blike, bleak.

senses.d: To close and reopen both eyes quickly.
ex: The loser in the staring game is the person who blinks first.

senses.d: To close and reopen one's eyes to remove (something) from on or around the eyes.
ex: She blinked her tears away.

senses.d: To wink; to twinkle with, or as with, the eye.
ex: One eye was blinking, and one leg was lame.

senses.d: To see with the eyes half shut, or indistinctly and with frequent winking, as a person with weak eyes.
ex: Show me thy chink, to blink through with mine eyne.

senses.d: To shine, especially with intermittent light; to twinkle; to flicker; to glimmer, as a lamp.
ex: The dew was falling fast, the stars began to blink.
The sun blinked fair on pool and stream.

senses.d: To glance.
To flash on and off at regular intervals.
ex: The blinking text on the screen was distracting.

senses.d: To flash headlights on a car at.
ex: An urban legend claims that gang members will attack anyone who blinks them.

senses.d: To send a signal with a lighting device.
ex: Don't come to the door until I blink twice.

senses.d: To perform the smallest action that could solicit a response.
ex: All the waiters in your grand cafe / Leave their tables when you blink.

senses.d: The act of quickly closing both eyes and opening them again.
